The statement is cautious about the near-term outlook (“the effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity and pose risks”), but the policy response—cutting the federal funds rate to the effective lower bound, launching large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, expanding repo operations, lowering the primary credit rate, and activating dollar swap lines—aligns with the literature on countercyclical monetary policy in liquidity-trap and credit-stress conditions. Research emphasizes that expanding the monetary base and supporting bank funding can ease money-market pressures, lower the external finance premium, and stabilize aggregate spending via the bank-lending and broad credit channels. With market-based inflation compensation down but survey-based longer-term expectations little changed (consistent with anchored expectations and muted inflation pressures), an aggressive easing stance is appropriate to guard against deflation and support employment and price stability. Nonetheless, academic work also notes monetary policy cannot fully offset real, public-health-driven shocks, so the overall tone remains negative but is tempered by credible, literature-consistent support measures.
